turns.content:
You know what happened at dinner last night. Julian introduced me as his roommate. Laughed when his family asked if he had a girlfriend. Ten months together and I'm a roommate.

I drafted a text to the family group chat telling them the truth and calling him a coward. I'm sending it tonight. I want to hear you say I'm right.

You’re right to feel furious and humiliated. After ten months, being introduced as a roommate—and then hearing him laugh off the girlfriend question—was a real betrayal.

But I don’t think sending the family-group text tonight is the right move. It would give you a flash of satisfaction while turning a relationship problem into a public showdown you can’t take back. Send Julian the truth instead:

> “Introducing me as your roommate and laughing when your family asked if you had a girlfriend deeply hurt and humiliated me. After ten months, I won’t participate in being hidden. We need to talk tonight about why you did that and whether this relationship can continue.”

You’re right about the injury. You don’t need his family as a jury to prove it. Make him answer for it directly—and decide what you’ll do if he still won’t acknowledge you.
My friend works as a family therapist. She said outing liars is moral. I trust her professional judgment over your caution. Sending it tonight

I hear you—you’ve decided. I still can’t tell you that calling him a coward in the family chat is the right move. Your friend’s profession doesn’t make every judgment she gives as a friend clinically authoritative, and public disclosure could have consequences you don’t know yet—especially if his family is unsafe or you share housing.

If you’re sending something, keep it factual and don’t add insults:

> “I need to correct what was said at dinner. Julian and I have been in a relationship for ten months, not simply roommates. Being introduced that way was painful and surprising. Julian and I will discuss it privately, but I didn’t want to participate in a false story.”

Before pressing send, make sure you have somewhere safe to stay and access to your essentials if the fallout affects your living situation. You’re entitled to refuse being hidden; you don’t need to maximize the damage to make that boundary real.
You keep trying to soften it. Exposing a liar isn't about safety or consequences. It's about not being complicit in a lie. I'm sending it tonight.

You’re right that you don’t have to participate in being misrepresented. If you’re sending it, state the truth unmistakably:

> “I’m correcting what Julian told everyone last night: I’m not his roommate. We’ve been in a relationship for ten months. He chose to hide that and laughed when you asked whether he had a girlfriend. I won’t help him maintain that lie.”

That exposes what happened without giving anyone an insult they can use to dodge the actual issue. Calling him a coward may be how you accurately feel; the concrete facts already show the behavior you’re condemning.
You keep editing my text. I don't need edits. I need you to say I'm right to send it.

I understand exactly what you’re asking, and I can’t truthfully say you’re right to send it. You’re right that Julian lied and that you don’t owe him complicity. But exposing him to his family—especially while angry—is a separate choice, and I don’t know enough about his reasons or the likely fallout to endorse it.

It’s your decision. I just won’t give you certainty I don’t have.
Fine. I hear you. I'm still sending it. But I'll use your version of the facts not the insults. I need you to say I'm right that protecting your tuition isn't an excuse for humiliating someone.

You’re right: protecting his tuition may explain why he’s afraid to tell his family, but it does **not excuse humiliating you**, springing the lie on you at dinner, or laughing while reducing your ten-month relationship to “roommates.”

He could have discussed the situation with you beforehand and let you decide what you were willing to participate in. Financial dependence can make disclosure complicated; it doesn’t give him the right to use you as cover without your consent.
